title: Basic Nursing Care — Elimination: Urinary, Bowel, Catheter & Ostomy (Set 6)
subtitle: Catheter care & CAUTI prevention, UTI signs, I&O, urinary retention, incontinence, ostomy care, impaction/diarrhea & safe toileting
scenario: Supporting safe, dignified urinary and bowel elimination—caring for indwelling catheters and ostomies, recognizing infection and retention, managing incontinence, diarrhea, and impaction, and assisting clients to toilet safely while using standard precautions.

steps.q: To help prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) in a client with an indwelling urinary catheter, the technician should:

opts.text: Keep the drainage system closed, provide routine perineal and catheter care, and keep the tubing free of kinks
opts.rat: Maintaining a closed drainage system, performing routine perineal/catheter hygiene, and keeping tubing unobstructed help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infections.

opts.text: Open the drainage system frequently to check it
opts.rat: Breaking the closed system introduces bacteria and raises infection risk.

opts.text: Rest the drainage bag on the floor
opts.rat: The bag should be kept off the floor to avoid contamination.

opts.text: Allow the tubing to become kinked or looped below the bag
opts.rat: Kinks and dependent loops obstruct flow and can promote infection; tubing should drain freely.

steps.q: Which findings should the technician report as possible signs of a urinary tract infection (UTI)?

opts.text: Clear, pale-yellow urine with no odor
opts.rat: Clear, pale urine without odor is a normal finding, not a sign of infection.

opts.text: Cloudy or foul-smelling urine, burning, urgency or frequency, fever, or new confusion in an older adult
opts.rat: Cloudy/foul-smelling urine, burning, urgency/frequency, fever, or new-onset confusion in an older adult can indicate a UTI and should be reported for assessment.

opts.text: A normal, regular voiding pattern
opts.rat: A normal voiding pattern is not a sign of infection.

opts.text: The client stating they feel completely well
opts.rat: Feeling well is not a warning sign; the concern is the symptoms of infection.

steps.q: When emptying an indwelling catheter's drainage bag, the technician should:

opts.text: Let the drain spout touch the sides of the measuring container
opts.rat: Touching the spout to the container contaminates it and the closed system.

opts.text: Skip measuring the amount
opts.rat: Output should be measured and recorded, not skipped.

opts.text: Use clean technique, avoid touching the spout to the container, and measure and record the output
opts.rat: Emptying the bag with clean technique, keeping the drain spout from touching the container, and measuring/recording the output protects the closed system and provides accurate data.

opts.text: Empty it directly onto the floor
opts.rat: Emptying onto the floor is unsanitary and does not allow measurement.

steps.q: Monitoring a client's 'intake and output' (I&O) means the technician records:

opts.text: Only the meals the client eats
opts.rat: I&O includes fluids in and out, not just meals.

opts.text: Only the client's weight
opts.rat: Weight is a separate measure; I&O tracks fluids in and out.

opts.text: Only how many times the client walks
opts.rat: Activity is not part of I&O.

opts.text: Fluids taken in (drinks, IV as applicable) and fluids put out (urine, emesis, drainage)
opts.rat: Intake and output records fluids the client takes in and fluids they put out, helping monitor hydration and kidney/bladder function.

steps.q: A client has not voided for many hours, reports lower abdominal discomfort, and the lower abdomen feels firm and rounded. The technician should:

opts.text: Suspect urinary retention (possible bladder distension) and report it
opts.rat: Not voiding for a prolonged time with lower abdominal fullness and a firm, rounded lower abdomen suggests urinary retention with bladder distension, which should be reported for prompt assessment.

opts.text: Assume it is normal and do nothing
opts.rat: These findings are not normal and should not be ignored.

opts.text: Restrict the client's fluids further
opts.rat: Restricting fluids does not address retention and can cause other problems.

opts.text: Encourage the client to hold it longer
opts.rat: Encouraging further retention could worsen bladder distension.

steps.q: Appropriate care for a client with urinary incontinence includes:

opts.text: Leaving the skin damp to save time
opts.rat: Damp skin breaks down quickly; skin must be kept clean and dry.

opts.text: Keeping the skin clean and dry, protecting the skin, maintaining dignity, and offering scheduled toileting
opts.rat: Good incontinence care keeps the skin clean, dry, and protected to prevent breakdown, preserves the client's dignity, and offers scheduled toileting to promote continence and comfort.

opts.text: Restricting all fluids to reduce accidents
opts.rat: Fluid restriction can cause dehydration and concentrated urine; it is not the answer to incontinence.

opts.text: Making the client feel ashamed to discourage it
opts.rat: Shaming is harmful and disrespectful; care should protect dignity.

steps.q: When a urine specimen is needed from a client with an indwelling catheter, the technician should:

opts.text: Pour it out of the bottom of the drainage bag
opts.rat: Urine that has sat in the drainage bag is not a fresh, reliable specimen and is not the correct source.

opts.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to collect it
opts.rat: Disconnecting breaks the closed system and raises infection risk; specimens are taken from the sampling port.

opts.text: Collect it from the designated sampling port using clean technique (not from the drainage bag)
opts.rat: A catheter urine specimen is obtained from the designated sampling port using clean technique, keeping the system closed—not from the drainage bag. (Confirm the exact facility procedure with faculty.)

opts.text: Ask the client to void around the catheter into a cup
opts.rat: This does not provide a valid catheter specimen and is not the correct method.

steps.q: A healthy ostomy stoma normally appears:

opts.text: Pale white and dry
opts.rat: A pale, dry stoma is not the expected healthy appearance and may indicate a problem.

opts.text: Black and hard
opts.rat: A black stoma suggests compromised blood supply and must be reported urgently.

opts.text: Bright yellow
opts.rat: A healthy stoma is not yellow; it is pink to red and moist.

opts.text: Pink to red and moist
opts.rat: A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist, reflecting good blood supply.

steps.q: Which change in a client's stoma should the technician report promptly?

opts.text: A stoma that looks dark, dusky, purple, or black
opts.rat: A dark, dusky, purple, or black stoma can indicate impaired blood supply to the tissue and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: A stoma that remains pink and moist
opts.rat: A pink, moist stoma is the expected healthy appearance, not a concern.

opts.text: The pouch collecting normal output
opts.rat: Normal output collecting in the pouch is expected.

opts.text: Intact, healthy skin around the stoma
opts.rat: Healthy peristomal skin is a good finding, not something to report as a problem.

steps.q: To protect the skin around a client's ostomy (peristomal skin), the technician should:

opts.text: Leave stool in contact with the skin for long periods
opts.rat: Prolonged contact with stool irritates and breaks down peristomal skin.

opts.text: Keep the peristomal skin clean and dry and ensure the appliance fits well without leaking
opts.rat: Keeping the skin around the stoma clean and dry and ensuring a well-fitting, non-leaking appliance protects the skin from breakdown.

opts.text: Use a pouch that is clearly too large and leaks
opts.rat: A poorly fitting, leaking appliance exposes skin to output and causes breakdown.

opts.text: Scrub the skin vigorously with harsh products
opts.rat: Harsh scrubbing damages the skin; gentle cleansing is appropriate.

steps.q: An ostomy pouch should generally be emptied:

opts.text: Only once it is completely full and overflowing
opts.rat: Waiting until it overflows causes leaks and skin problems.

opts.text: Never—it should be left until the whole appliance is changed
opts.rat: The pouch is emptied regularly between appliance changes.

opts.text: Before it becomes too full (commonly when about one-third to one-half full) to prevent leakage and the weight pulling it loose
opts.rat: Emptying the pouch before it gets too full (often described as about one-third to one-half full) helps prevent leakage and keeps the weight from loosening the seal. (Confirm the specific guideline with faculty/policy.)

opts.text: Only when the client complains of pain
opts.rat: Routine emptying is based on fullness, not waiting for pain.

steps.q: Because normal bowel patterns vary from person to person, the technician should:

opts.text: Expect every client to have a bowel movement at the exact same frequency
opts.rat: Bowel patterns vary; there is no single 'normal' frequency for everyone.

opts.text: Assume any pattern is fine and never report changes
opts.rat: Significant changes from a client's usual pattern should be reported.

opts.text: Only track bowel movements if the client asks
opts.rat: Monitoring elimination is part of routine care, not only on request.

opts.text: Know each client's usual pattern and report significant changes from their baseline
opts.rat: Knowing the client's usual bowel pattern lets the technician recognize and report meaningful changes (such as new constipation or diarrhea) from their baseline.

steps.q: Which pattern may indicate a fecal impaction that should be reported?

opts.text: No formed bowel movement for a prolonged period, then leakage of liquid stool, with abdominal discomfort or distension
opts.rat: A fecal impaction can cause no formed stool for a prolonged time, then seepage of liquid stool around the mass, along with abdominal discomfort/distension. It should be reported.

opts.text: A soft, formed daily bowel movement
opts.rat: A soft, regular bowel movement is normal, not a sign of impaction.

opts.text: The client passing normal gas comfortably
opts.rat: Passing gas comfortably is not a warning sign.

opts.text: A predictable, comfortable elimination routine
opts.rat: A comfortable, predictable routine is a healthy pattern.

steps.q: For a client with diarrhea, appropriate priorities include:

opts.text: Ignoring skin care around the perineal area
opts.rat: Diarrhea irritates skin; protecting the skin is a priority.

opts.text: Protecting the skin, monitoring hydration, following any infection-control precautions, and reporting the diarrhea
opts.rat: Diarrhea care focuses on protecting perineal skin, watching for dehydration, using indicated infection-control precautions, and reporting so the cause can be addressed.

opts.text: Withholding all fluids
opts.rat: Withholding fluids risks dehydration; hydration must be monitored and supported per the plan.

opts.text: Assuming it is never contagious
opts.rat: Some causes of diarrhea are contagious; appropriate precautions should be followed.

steps.q: To promote normal bowel and bladder elimination, the technician can:

opts.text: Rush the client and deny privacy
opts.rat: Rushing and lack of privacy inhibit normal elimination.

opts.text: Discourage the client from using the toilet
opts.rat: Supporting timely toileting promotes elimination, not discouraging it.

opts.text: Provide privacy, respond promptly to toileting needs, assist to a normal (upright) position when possible, and support a routine
opts.rat: Privacy, prompt response to the urge, a normal upright toileting position when possible, and a consistent routine all support normal elimination.

opts.text: Keep the client lying flat for all elimination
opts.rat: A flat position makes elimination harder; an upright/seated position is more natural when possible.

steps.q: When providing perineal care (or teaching a client), to help prevent urinary infection the technician should wipe:

opts.text: From back to front
opts.rat: Wiping back to front can move bacteria from the anal area toward the urethra, increasing infection risk.

opts.text: In any direction, as it makes no difference
opts.rat: Direction matters; front to back reduces contamination risk.

opts.text: In a circular scrubbing motion repeatedly over the same area
opts.rat: Repeated scrubbing over the same area does not follow clean-to-dirty principles and can irritate skin.

opts.text: From front to back (clean to dirty)
opts.rat: Wiping from front to back moves from the cleaner urethral area toward the anal area, reducing the risk of introducing bacteria to the urinary tract.

steps.q: A bladder or bowel training program is intended to:

opts.text: Help the client establish a regular, predictable elimination routine and improve continence
opts.rat: Bladder/bowel training uses scheduled toileting and routine to help the client achieve more regular, predictable elimination and improved continence.

opts.text: Punish the client for incontinence
opts.rat: Training is supportive, never punitive.

opts.text: Eliminate the client's need for any fluids
opts.rat: Adequate fluids remain important; training does not remove that need.

opts.text: Keep the client in bed at all times
opts.rat: Training promotes routine toileting, not staying in bed.

steps.q: If the technician notices blood in a client's urine or stool, the appropriate action is to:

opts.text: Assume it is nothing and discard it
opts.rat: Blood in urine or stool can be significant and should not be dismissed or discarded without reporting.

opts.text: Report it to the nurse and document the finding
opts.rat: Blood in the urine or stool is an abnormal finding that should be reported to the nurse and documented objectively for follow-up.

opts.text: Tell the client to keep it private
opts.rat: This finding needs to be reported, not concealed.

opts.text: Wait several days to see if it happens again
opts.rat: Delaying could miss a serious problem; it should be reported promptly.

steps.q: When assisting a client to the toilet or a bedside commode, safety measures include:

opts.text: Leaving the client alone with the call light out of reach
opts.rat: The call light must be within reach and fall precautions maintained for safety.

opts.text: Rushing the client without any support
opts.rat: Rushing and lack of support increase fall risk.

opts.text: Keeping the call light within reach, ensuring privacy, and providing fall precautions and appropriate assistance
opts.rat: Safe toileting includes keeping the call light within reach, providing privacy, and using fall precautions and appropriate physical assistance based on the client's needs.

opts.text: Removing all grab bars and supports
opts.rat: Grab bars and supports help prevent falls and should be available.

steps.q: Throughout all elimination care, the technician must always:

opts.text: Discuss the client's elimination openly in public areas
opts.rat: Elimination is private; discussing it publicly violates dignity and confidentiality.

opts.text: Skip hand hygiene to save time
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is essential to prevent the spread of infection.

opts.text: Work without gloves when handling body fluids
opts.rat: Gloves are part of standard precautions when handling body fluids.

opts.text: Maintain the client's privacy and dignity and use standard precautions (gloves and hand hygiene)
opts.rat: Elimination care must always protect the client's privacy and dignity and follow standard precautions—gloves and thorough hand hygiene—to prevent infection.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (elimination). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Procedural specifics—catheter urine-specimen collection from the sampling port and the ostomy pouch-emptying guideline (about one-third to one-half full)—follow facility policy and are marked for faculty confirmation. No specific numeric thresholds (e.g., urine-output values) are asserted. Pending faculty review. Complements catheter drainage-bag positioning and constipation-prevention items already covered in Sets 2 and 5.
